resources.title: dbt Test Writer
resources.tagline: Generate the minimum test set that actually protects a model.
resources.description: Proposes dbt tests ranked by blast radius: uniqueness/not-null on the grain key, accepted values on enums, relationships on foreign keys, and freshness on sources.
learning_objectives: Rank tests by the cost of the failure they prevent
Write a custom singular test
Wire freshness on a source
resources.body:
# dbt Test Writer

## Rank by blast radius, not by effort
1. `unique` + `not_null` on the grain key — the model is meaningless without it.
2. `relationships` on every foreign key — catches broken joins upstream.
3. `accepted_values` on low-cardinality enums — catches upstream renames.
4. `freshness` on sources — catches a stalled extractor, the #1 silent outage.

## Avoid
- Row-count equality tests on raw sources: they flake.
- Testing a column nobody reads.
- `warn` severity on a correctness test nobody will see.
resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Incident Postmortem Writer
resources.tagline: Turn a pipeline incident into a blameless postmortem with real action items.
resources.description: Structures incident notes into a blameless postmortem: timeline, impact, detection gap, contributing factors, and action items with owners and dates.
learning_objectives: Write a blameless timeline
Separate trigger from contributing factors
Convert findings into dated, owned action items
resources.body:
# Incident Postmortem Writer

## Structure
1. **Impact** — who/what, in business terms, with a duration.
2. **Timeline** — timestamped, factual, no blame.
3. **Detection** — how we found out; if a human told us, that's a gap.
4. **Contributing factors** — plural; incidents are rarely single-cause.
5. **Action items** — each with an owner and a date, and a "done" definition.

## Anti-pattern
"Be more careful" is not an action item. Change the system so a careful mistake
is harmless.
resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: SQL Review
resources.tagline: A review pass that catches correctness bugs before the query reaches production.
resources.description: Reviews a SQL statement for fan-out joins, NULL-unsafe predicates, implicit casts, non-deterministic ordering, and functions that silently change grain.
learning_objectives: Prove a join cannot fan out before writing it
Spot NULL-unsafe `NOT IN` and `=` predicates
State the grain of a result set in one sentence
resources.body:
# SQL Review

## The first question
*What is the grain of this result?* If the author can't answer, stop.

## Rules
1. Every join states its cardinality (1:1, N:1, N:N) and justifies it.
2. `NOT IN (subquery)` is banned where the subquery can return NULL — use `NOT EXISTS`.
3. Comparisons across types must be explicit casts, not implicit.
4. `ORDER BY` without `LIMIT` in a view is meaningless — drop it.
5. `SELECT *` in a persisted model freezes an unstable schema.

## Deliverable
Findings with the exact predicate, the failure case, and a rewritten clause.
resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Airflow DAG Reviewer
resources.tagline: Review a DAG for idempotency, retry safety, and backfill behaviour.
resources.description: Checks a DAG for non-idempotent tasks, unsafe retries, missing catchup policy, ambiguous catchup/backfill semantics and unbounded concurrency.
learning_objectives: Make every task safe to re-run
Choose retries and timeouts deliberately
Predict what a backfill will do before running it
resources.body:
# Airflow DAG Reviewer

## The idempotency test
"If this task runs twice for the same logical date, is the output the same?"
If no, fix it before anything else — retries will happen.

## Checklist
1. Every task writes to a partition keyed by the logical date, or uses MERGE.
2. `catchup` is a deliberate choice, not a default.
3. Retries have a backoff; a task that retries instantly will hammer a downstream.
4. `max_active_runs` and pool limits prevent a backfill from starving the daily run.
5. Sensors use `reschedule`, not `poke`, so they don't hold a worker slot.
resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Athena Partition Advisor
resources.tagline: Cut scanned bytes — the only thing Athena bills you for.
resources.description: Recommends partition projection, bucketing or file-layout changes to reduce Athena bytes-scanned, and writes the projection DDL.
learning_objectives: Read the scanned-bytes metric per query
Apply partition projection for high-cardinality columns
Compact small files to cut per-request overhead
resources.body:
# Athena Partition Advisor

## Bill model
You pay per TB scanned. Every recommendation is judged by "does this reduce
bytes scanned?" — nothing else matters.

## Levers, in order
1. Partition on the dominant filter column (usually date).
2. Partition projection instead of `MSCK REPAIR` for predictable layouts.
3. Compact small files — per-file overhead dominates at < 16 MB.
4. Columnar + compression (Parquet + snappy/zstd) — 10-100x vs CSV.
resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: AWS Glue Job Reviewer
resources.tagline: Review a Glue job for cost, DPU sizing, and bookmarks correctness.
resources.description: Reviews Glue/Spark jobs for worker sizing, job bookmarks, partition pruning, and the catalogue/schema pitfalls that cause silent full reprocessing.
learning_objectives: Size Glue workers from data volume, not habit
Use job bookmarks correctly
Avoid full-table reprocessing from catalogue mistakes
resources.body:
# AWS Glue Job Reviewer

## Sizing
Start at 2x the number of input files' partitions, then watch the task histogram.
Over-provisioned workers are the most common Glue cost leak.

## Bookmarks
A bookmark only helps if the input path layout is stable. A renamed prefix
silently resets the bookmark → full reprocess.

## Catalogue trap
If the Glue Data Catalog schema drifts from the actual Parquet schema, readers
drop columns silently. Diff the catalogue schema against the file footer.
resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Cost Unit-Economics Reporter
resources.tagline: Attribute pipeline cost per row, per table, per team.
resources.description: Turns cluster/warehouse billing into unit economics (cost per 1M rows, per run, per model) so a 4x regression shows up as a number, not a surprise invoice.
learning_objectives: Attribute compute cost to a pipeline run
Define a unit metric that resists regressions
Set an alert on cost-per-run, not on total spend
resources.body:
# Cost Unit-Economics Reporter

## Unit metrics that don't lie
- $ per pipeline run (stable denominator)
- $ per 1M rows processed
- DBU/credits per model build

## Why total spend is the wrong alert
Total spend rises with growth and hides regressions. Cost-per-unit is flat when
growth is healthy and spikes the day a join starts fanning out.

resources.title: Data Contract Author
resources.tagline: Turn a vague producer/consumer agreement into an enforceable contract.
resources.description: Drafts a data contract (schema, semantics, freshness SLA, ownership, breaking- change policy) and the tests that enforce it in CI.
learning_objectives: Specify a freshness and completeness SLA
Encode a contract as executable tests
Define a breaking-change policy consumers can rely on
resources.body:
# Data Contract Author

## A contract has six parts
1. Owner (a team, with an on-call).
2. Schema (typed, versioned).
3. Semantics (what each field *means*, units, nullability).
4. SLA (freshness, completeness).
5. Breaking-change policy (notice period, deprecation path).
6. Enforcement (which CI test fails on violation).

## Rule
A contract with no enforcement is documentation. Documentation is not a contract.
resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: dbt Model Review
resources.tagline: Review a dbt model for grain, materialisation, and incremental correctness.
resources.description: Checks a dbt model's grain statement, ref/dependency hygiene, incremental strategy and late-arriving-data handling, then proposes a test set.
learning_objectives: State a model's grain and match it to its unique key test
Choose table vs incremental vs view deliberately
Handle late data in an incremental model
resources.body:
# dbt Model Review

## Grain first
Every model must answer: "one row = one ___". The `unique` test goes on that key.

## Materialisation picker
- `view` — cheap, and the model is small or rarely queried.
- `table` — the source is huge and consumers need speed.
- `incremental` — the source grows monotonically and you can define the watermark.

## Incremental traps
1. Late-arriving rows older than the watermark are silently dropped. Add a
   lookback window (e.g. `>= max(updated_at) - interval '3 days'`).
2. `is_incremental()` must guard the filter or every full run is a full reload.
3. Deletes never arrive. Decide explicitly: soft-delete, or periodic full-refresh.
resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Delta Optimization Advisor
resources.tagline: OPTIMIZE, Z-ORDER, or nothing — decide with data, not vibes.
resources.description: Reads Delta table history and file statistics to decide between OPTIMIZE, Z-ORDER, liquid clustering and partitioning changes.
learning_objectives: Decide if a table needs OPTIMIZE from file stats
Choose Z-ORDER columns from query predicates
Know when liquid clustering beats partitioning
resources.body:
# Delta Optimization Advisor

## Decide
- Files < 32 MB and many → `OPTIMIZE`.
- Queries filter on 1-2 high-cardinality columns → `ZORDER BY` those columns.
- High-cardinality, many predicates, frequent writes → liquid clustering.
- Predicate on one low-cardinality column (date) → partition (or leave it; Delta
  handles pruning well already).

## Measure
Compare `numFiles` and query `bytes scanned` before and after. If scanning
didn't drop, the Z-ORDER was on the wrong columns.

resources.title: Lineage Explainer
resources.tagline: Answer "what breaks if I change this column?" with evidence.
resources.description: Traces column-level lineage from an asset to its upstream sources and downstream consumers, and reports the impact set for a proposed change.
learning_objectives: Read the lineages of an asset from a lineage store
Compute a downstream impact set
Distinguish technical from business lineage
resources.body:
# Lineage Explainer

## Two questions, two graphs
- **Technical lineage** — which tables/jobs depend on this column.
- **Business lineage** — which metrics/reports depend on it.

A breaking change needs both, because a CFO does not read table names.

## Impact set
Walk downstream from the changed node, stopping at published marts. Report
owner, criticality, and the earliest SLA that will break.

resources.title: PII Classifier
resources.tagline: Find PII in a dataset and propose the masking policy.
resources.description: Scans column names and sample values for PII categories, then proposes classification tags and a masking/pseudonymisation policy.
learning_objectives: Classify columns into PII categories
Choose masking vs hashing vs tokenisation
Record a data-classification tag
resources.body:
# PII Classifier

## Caution
Sampling real data to find PII is itself a privacy action. Prefer metadata-only
heuristics first; only sample with authorisation, and never persist samples.

## Categories
Direct identifiers (name, email, phone, national ID), quasi-identifiers
(postcode, DOB), sensitive attributes (health, financial), and free text
(which can contain anything).

## Policy mapping
Direct → mask or tokenise. Quasi → generalise. Free text → never expose raw in
analytics; store separately with restricted access.

resources.title: Pipeline Test Author
resources.tagline: Write integration tests for a pipeline that run in seconds, offline.
resources.description: Builds a local DuckDB/pyarrow harness with tiny fixtures so pipeline logic is testable in CI without a cluster, and asserts on invariants, not snapshots.
learning_objectives: Test a transform without a Spark cluster
Assert invariants instead of golden files
Make a pipeline test deterministic
resources.body:
# Pipeline Test Author

## The harness
Keep fixtures as 3-10 row Parquet/CSV files under `tests/data/`. Load them with
DuckDB or pyarrow. No cluster, no network, < 2s.

## Assert invariants, not snapshots
- `count(*)` is stable across a re-run (idempotency)
- no nulls in the grain key
- sum(revenue) equals the source sum within tolerance
- a quarantined row never appears in the published table

## Rule
If a test needs the network or a running warehouse, it is not a unit test.

resources.title: Schema Change Contract Review
resources.tagline: Classify a schema change as safe, risky, or breaking — before it ships.
resources.description: Diffs an old and new schema, classifies the change (compatible / risky / breaking) against consumers, and produces the migration and comms plan.
learning_objectives: Apply backward/forward compatibility rules to a diff
Detect a breaking change hidden behind a "safe" rename
Write a deprecation plan with dates
resources.body:
# Schema Change Contract Review

## Classification
- **Compatible** — new nullable column, widened type that preserves values.
- **Risky** — narrowing a type, adding a NOT NULL without a default, changing units.
- **Breaking** — rename, remove, or semantic change to an existing column.

## The hidden breaking change
A rename + a new column with the old name looks compatible to a schema differ
but breaks every consumer that read the old semantics. Always diff *semantics*,
not just names.

## Migration skeleton
Add → dual-write → backfill → announce → migrate consumers → remove (dated).
resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Spark Data Quality Review
resources.tagline: Audit a PySpark job for silent data-quality failures before it ships.
resources.description: A review skill an agent runs against a Spark/PySpark transform. It checks null propagation, join fan-out, silent type coercion, non-deterministic row counts and missing post-write assertions, then reports findings as a diff-level list.
learning_objectives: Identify the five classes of silent failure in a Spark transform
Add pre/post row-count and null assertions to a job
Recognise join fan-out caused by non-unique keys
resources.body:
# Spark Data Quality Review

## When to use
Run this when a PySpark transform is about to be merged, or when a downstream
table's row count changed without a code change.

## Check order
1. **Null propagation** — every outer join introduces nullable right-side keys.
   Confirm downstream code coalesces or filters them.
2. **Join fan-out** — assert key uniqueness on the intended 1-side before joining.
3. **Silent coercion** — `cast` failures return null, not errors. Prefer `try_cast`
   and count the nulls it produces.
4. **Non-determinism** — `dropDuplicates` without a sort key keeps an arbitrary row.
5. **Missing assertions** — every write should be followed by a row-count and a
   null-rate check on the primary key.

## Output
A findings list: `severity | file:line | rule | suggested patch`.

resources.title: SQL Query Plan Explainer
resources.tagline: Translate an EXPLAIN plan into plain language and the one change worth making.
resources.description: Reads EXPLAIN / EXPLAIN ANALYZE output and explains scans, joins, spills and estimated-vs-actual row skew, then proposes the single highest-impact change.
learning_objectives: Read a plan bottom-up and name the expensive node
Detect cardinality misestimation from stale statistics
Decide between an index, a rewrite, or a stats refresh
resources.body:
# SQL Query Plan Explainer

## Method
1. Read bottom-up; the deepest node is the first data touched.
2. Compare `rows` (estimate) to `actual rows`. >10x off means stale stats.
3. Look for `Seq Scan` on a large table that should use an index.
4. Look for `Sort` / `Hash` spilling to disk (`disk usage` in the plan).

## Output
One sentence per expensive node, then exactly one recommended change with
the expected effect and a way to measure it.

resources.body:
# Backfill Planner

## Before running anything
1. **Why** — which dates are wrong, and what does "correct" look like?
2. **Blast radius** — list every downstream model/table that reads the target.
3. **Contention** — will this run beside the daily job? At what hour is the cluster idle?
4. **Idempotency** — can each date be re-run safely?
5. **Rollback** — snapshot the target, or write to a shadow table first.

## Execution
Backfill in date batches, smallest first, validating a sample after each batch.

resources.tagline: Design a correct upsert/delete merge from a change stream.
resources.description: Produces a MERGE (or Delta/Iceberg merge) that applies inserts, updates and deletes from a CDC stream correctly, including out-of-order events and tombstones.
learning_objectives: Order change events deterministically
Handle deletes (tombstones) without losing history
Make the merge idempotent under replay
resources.body:
# CDC Merge Designer

## Ordering
Events arrive out of order. Rank by `(lsn, ts_ms)` — never by ingestion time.

## Deduplicate before merging
Keep the latest event per primary key with a window function, then merge once.

## Deletes
A delete is an event with `op = 'd'`. Two valid choices:
- hard delete on merge, or
- soft delete + `_deleted_at` (required if you need history or audit).

## Idempotency
Re-running the same micro-batch must produce the same table. Ranking by LSN
guarantees this; ranking by arrival time does not.

resources.description: Diagnoses small-file and manifest bloat and generates the compaction, snapshot expiry and orphan-file cleanup plan for an Iceberg table.
learning_objectives: Read an Iceberg metadata table to size the problem
Pick a compaction strategy and rewrite interval
Expire snapshots without breaking time travel
resources.body:
# Iceberg Table Maintenance

## Diagnose from metadata
```sql
SELECT count(*) files, avg(file_size_in_bytes)/1e6 avg_mb
FROM db.tbl.files;
```
avg_mb < 32 and a growing count → compact.

## Plan
1. `rewrite_data_files` with a target size (128-256 MB).
2. `rewrite_manifests` when the manifest list is huge.
3. `expire_snapshots` older than the retention window — but keep at least one
   full snapshot for time travel.
4. `remove_orphan_files` on a schedule, with a safety margin.

## Do not
Run compaction during peak ingestion; it conflicts with concurrent writers.

resources.tagline: Decide whether lag is a capacity problem, a poison message, or skew.
resources.description: Triages consumer lag from the consumer-group offsets: distinguishing a slow consumer, a partitioned hot key, a rebalance storm, and a poison-pill retry loop.
learning_objectives: Read per-partition lag to separate skew from throughput
Detect a rebalance loop from consumer-group state
Find the poison message from retry counts
resources.body:
# Kafka Consumer Lag Triage

## Three questions
1. Is lag rising, flat, or falling? Flat at a high number is fine; rising is not.
2. Is lag even across partitions? Skew means a hot key, not capacity.
3. Is the consumer group stable? Frequent `PreparingRebalance` is the real bug.

## Signatures
- Lag on one partition only → key skew; re-key or increase partitions.
- All partitions rising, CPU low → downstream (DB/API) is the bottleneck.
- Lag resets to zero then climbs → rebalance loop; check `session.timeout.ms`.
- One offset stuck, others advance → poison message in a retry loop.

## Never
Do not "fix" lag by resetting offsets. That is data loss wearing a hat.

learning_objectives: Read a tool schema and predict its side effects

Write a least-privilege MCP configuration
resources.body:
# MCP Tool Contract Auditor

## Classify every tool
- **Read** — safe, still logs the data it can reach.
- **Write** — can mutate state; needs a sandbox or a dry-run.
- **Destructive** — delete/drop/truncate; require human confirmation.
- **Spend** — provisions resources or runs billable queries.
- **Exfiltrate** — can send data to an external network.

## Deliverable
A table of tools by class, then a config that grants only the Read/Write tools
the task needs. Never connect an unvetted server with broad credentials.

resources.title: Spark Cost Regression Guard
resources.tagline: Detect the 4x cost jump in CI, before it reaches the invoice.
resources.description: Compares a job's shuffle/spill/scan metrics against a stored baseline and fails the change if cost-per-run regresses beyond a threshold, with the diff explained.
learning_objectives: Capture cost-relevant metrics from a Spark run
Store and compare a baseline
Explain which stage caused a regression
resources.body:
# Spark Cost Regression Guard

## Metrics worth baselining
shuffle read/write bytes, spill (disk) bytes, task count, max task duration,
input bytes. These predict cost far better than wall-clock time.

## Threshold
Fail if any metric grows > 25% vs the stored median of the last 5 runs. A 4x
regression is then caught at 1.25x, in CI, for free.

## Explain the diff
Name the stage whose metric moved, and whether it was a join, an aggregation,
or a partition count change.

resources.title: Spark Skew Diagnosis
resources.tagline: Turn "one task is 40 minutes behind" into a named root cause and a fix.
resources.description: Walks an agent through reading the Spark UI/event log to distinguish key skew, partition skew, and shuffle-write amplification, then selects between salting, AQE skew join, broadcast, and repartition strategies.
learning_objectives: Read task-level duration histograms to confirm skew
Choose between AQE skew join, salting and broadcast
Reproduce skew locally with a bounded dataset
resources.body:
# Spark Skew Diagnosis

## Signals
- Median task duration ~p50, but p99 is 30x+ → key skew.
- All tasks slow and shuffle read is huge → partition/scan problem, not skew.
- One executor at 100% while others idle → hot partition.

## Decision order
1. Confirm with `spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled=true` — if it fixes it, ship that.
2. If not, salt the hot key on both sides and aggregate twice.
3. Broadcast only if the small side is < 100 MB *after* filtering.
4. Never `repartition(1)` to "fix" skew; it serialises the stage.

## Evidence to attach
The task-duration histogram, the shuffle read/write bytes, and the top-10 keys
by row count — the review is not complete without them.

resources.tagline: Choose warehouse size, clustering keys, and caching — measured.
resources.description: Advises on Snowflake/BigQuery/Redshift tuning: clustering keys, warehouse sizing, result caching, and the difference between a scan problem and a compute problem.
learning_objectives: Separate scan inefficiency from compute inefficiency
Choose a clustering key from predicate selectivity

resources.body:
# Warehouse Clustering Advisor

## Diagnose first
- Query scans far more partitions than it needs → clustering/partition problem.
- Scan is optimal but the query waits → warehouse sizing or concurrency problem.

## Clustering key choice
Pick the column that appears in the WHERE clause of the *most expensive* queries,
with reasonable cardinality. Order matters: put the most selective first.

## Right-sizing from queue time
If queue time >> execution time for short queries, scale out (more clusters),
not up (bigger warehouse). Different problems, different knobs.

symptoms: Cluster/DBU spend for one job quadrupled overnight
Invoice alert, or a cost-per-run dashboard spike
Often no functional change was noticed
possible_causes: A join started fanning out, exploding row counts mid-stage
A partition filter was dropped (full history re-read)
Small-file explosion after a partitioning change
Autoscaling widened because a stage became slow (compounding loop)
diagnosis: Diff shuffle write bytes and input bytes for the job run-over-run.
Compare output row counts before/after the join, per stage.
Check whether the partition predicate still prunes (bytes scanned).
commands: SELECT count(*) FROM stage_output_pre JOIN ... -- compare to source count
fix: Fan-out → dedupe the many-side on the join key before joining.
Lost filter → restore the partition predicate and re-run.
Small files → OPTIMIZE/compact, then re-run.
prevention: Cost-per-run unit metric with a 25% regression alarm.
CI guard on shuffle/scan metrics (hook-spark-cost-check).
monitoring: $ per run, shuffle write bytes, input bytes, output rows

resources.title: dbt as Models + Tests + Docs
resources.description: Transformation logic lives in untested, undocumented SQL scattered across scripts.
resources.summary: Transformation logic lives in untested, undocumented SQL scattered across scripts.
resources.problem: Transformation logic lives in untested, undocumented SQL scattered across scripts.
resources.context: Warehouse transformation with recurring models and consumers.
forces: New joiners need to understand the lineage
resources.solution:
Every model is code with three faces:
  model (SQL) + tests (schema.yml) + docs (descriptions)
`ref()` builds the DAG; tests encode the invariants; descriptions are the docs
site consumers actually read. Materialisation is a deliberate choice per model.
resources.diagram:
source ─▶ stg_* ─▶ int_* ─▶ fct_*/dim_* ─▶ marts
          (tests + docs on every node)
tradeoffs: pro: testable, reviewable, self-documenting transformations
con: dbt adds a layer to learn; over-testing becomes slow CI

resources.title: Idempotent Partition Overwrite
resources.description: Retries and backfills duplicate or corrupt data because writes are appends.
resources.summary: Retries and backfills duplicate or corrupt data because writes are appends.
resources.problem: Retries and backfills duplicate or corrupt data because writes are appends.
resources.context: Any batch pipeline that may be re-run for the same logical date.
resources.solution:
Make each run write the complete result for its logical partition and replace
that partition atomically. Never append to a partition you can recompute.
`INSERT OVERWRITE partition(dt=...)` or Delta/Iceberg replace-where do this.
The invariant: running the same date twice yields identical output.
resources.diagram:
run(dt=2026-09-01) ─▶ [compute] ─▶ OVERWRITE dt=2026-09-01
run(dt=2026-09-01) ─▶ [compute] ─▶ OVERWRITE dt=2026-09-01  (same result)
tradeoffs: pro: retries and backfills are safe by construction
con: requires a well-defined logical partition; hard for cross-partition state
when_not: Streaming writes with no partition boundary (use MERGE/upsert instead)

resources.title: Medallion Zones (raw / curated / serving)
resources.description: Object storage gives you a place to put files but no structure for trust or ownership.
resources.summary: Object storage gives you a place to put files but no structure for trust or ownership.
resources.problem: Object storage gives you a place to put files but no structure for trust or ownership.
resources.context: A lake or lakehouse where many teams write and read, and consumers need to know how far to trust a table.
forces: Consumers want clean, typed, tested tables
resources.solution:
Three zones with explicit contracts between them.
  raw/       — immutable, exactly as received; never edited; schema-on-read.
  curated/   — cleaned, typed, deduplicated; partitioned; quality-gated.
  serving/   — modelled marts optimised for consumption; SLA-bearing.
Each zone has a different retention, quality bar and owner. Promotion between
zones is a pipeline step with a gate, not a copy.
tradeoffs: pro: clear trust boundary, cheap reprocessing from raw
con: multiple copies, more storage and more pipelines to run
watch: don't let curated become a dumping ground; enforce the gate
when_to_use: Multiple consumers with different quality needs
You need an audit trail to the source
when_not: A single small pipeline with one consumer
When storage cost dominates and copies are wasteful

resources.title: Agent-in-the-Loop Review
resources.description: Coding agents can do real data-engineering work, but can also ship a schema change or drop a table.
resources.summary: Coding agents can do real data-engineering work, but can also ship a schema change or drop a table.
resources.problem: Coding agents can do real data-engineering work, but can also ship a schema change or drop a table.
resources.context: Using coding agents against real data repositories and warehouses.
forces: Trust must be earned per action
resources.solution:
Separate read/recommend from write/execute.
  read ─▶ recommend ─▶ human approves ─▶ execute (scoped, logged)
Constrain the agent with read-only credentials plus MCP servers limited to the
needed tools. Encode the safety policy as hooks (destructive SQL guard, prod
write confirmation), and keep a human in the loop for anything irreversible.
resources.diagram:
agent ─(read tools)─▶ analysis ─▶ proposal ─▶ ⛔ human gate ─▶ scoped write
                                      └─ hooks enforce policy ─┘
tradeoffs: pro: agent velocity with bounded, auditable blast radius
con: the human gate adds friction; requires a real permission model
when_not: A purely local sandbox with no real data

resources.title: Compaction & File-Size Management
resources.description: High-frequency writes shatter a table into thousands of tiny files and queries crawl.
resources.summary: High-frequency writes shatter a table into thousands of tiny files and queries crawl.
resources.problem: High-frequency writes shatter a table into thousands of tiny files and queries crawl.
resources.context: A lakehouse table written by micro-batches or streaming.
resources.solution:
Separate the write path from the layout path.
  writes ─▶ many small files ─▶ [scheduled compaction] ─▶ 128-256 MB files
Compact on a schedule (or auto-compact), targeting a file size that matches your
read pattern. Rewrite manifests when metadata grows. Do it outside the ingestion
window so compaction and writers don't contend.
tradeoffs: pro: fast reads without slowing writes
con: compaction costs compute and can conflict with concurrent writers
when_not: Low-frequency bulk writes that already produce large files

resources.title: Contracts as a Quality Gate
resources.description: Producers change schemas and semantics with no notice; consumers break in production.
resources.summary: Producers change schemas and semantics with no notice; consumers break in production.
resources.problem: Producers change schemas and semantics with no notice; consumers break in production.
resources.context: Multiple teams, a shared data platform, and a catalogue or registry of assets.
forces: Nobody reads a wiki on time
resources.solution:
A contract is code that runs in the producer's CI.
  contract ─▶ compatibility check (CI) ─▶ build ─▶ publish ─▶ consumers
Additive changes pass. Breaking changes require a dated deprecation plan.
The gate lives where the change is made (producer CI), not in the consumer's
runtime — the cheapest place to catch it is before merge.
resources.diagram:
producer change ─▶ [contract CI] ─┬─ compatible ─▶ deploy
                                  └─ breaking ─▶ blocked + plan required
tradeoffs: pro: failures caught pre-merge, at the producer
con: producers carry process overhead; needs buy-in
when_not: A single team owning the whole chain

resources.title: Cost Guardrails
resources.description: A working pipeline silently becomes expensive and nobody notices until the invoice.
resources.summary: A working pipeline silently becomes expensive and nobody notices until the invoice.
resources.problem: A working pipeline silently becomes expensive and nobody notices until the invoice.
resources.context: Any cloud data platform with variable compute.
resources.solution:
Instrument, attribute, then guard.
  1. unit metric per pipeline ($ per run, per 1M rows)
  2. baseline the last N runs
  3. fail CI on regression > threshold
  4. hard caps (warehouse resource monitors, quota limits)
Alert on the *unit* metric, never on total spend, so healthy growth doesn't page
anyone and a regression does.
resources.diagram:
run ─▶ metrics ─▶ unit metric ─┬─ within baseline ─▶ pass
                                └─ regressed ─▶ fail CI / alert
tradeoffs: pro: cheap early detection, no invoice surprises
con: needs metrics plumbing and a baseline to be maintained
when_to_use: Any pipeline with variable compute cost

resources.title: Dimensional Model (star schema)
resources.description: Analysts re-derive the same joins and disagree on metric definitions.
resources.summary: Analysts re-derive the same joins and disagree on metric definitions.
resources.problem: Analysts re-derive the same joins and disagree on metric definitions.
resources.context: A warehouse serving BI and analytics with recurring query patterns.
resources.solution:
Facts (events/measures) surrounded by conformed dimensions (context).
  fct_orders (grain: one row per order line)
    ├─ dim_customer (SCD2 for history)
    ├─ dim_product
    └─ dim_date
Declare the fact grain explicitly. Conform dimensions across facts so they can
be combined. Use slowly-changing-dimension type 2 when an attribute's history
must be preserved at the point of the fact.
tradeoffs: pro: fast, intuitive, consistent; BI-friendly
con: less flexible for rare queries; ETL to maintain SCDs
when_not: Rapidly changing source schemas (consider Data Vault)

resources.title: Incremental Batch with a Watermark
resources.description: Full reloads are too slow and too expensive once a table grows past millions of rows.
resources.summary: Full reloads are too slow and too expensive once a table grows past millions of rows.
resources.problem: Full reloads are too slow and too expensive once a table grows past millions of rows.
resources.context: A batch pipeline reading an append-mostly source that has an updated_at/event time.
forces: Late-arriving rows must not be lost
resources.solution:
Process a window that ends at a watermark and starts a lookback before it.
  scan from (max(watermark) - lookback) to now
The lookback absorbs late arrivals; the watermark bounds the work. Write
idempotently (partition overwrite or MERGE) so a re-run is safe. Handle deletes
explicitly (soft-delete or periodic full refresh) — they don't arrive in an
append-only stream.
tradeoffs: pro: cost scales with new data, not history
con: lookback trades correctness for cost; too short loses late rows
watch: a naive is_incremental() without a lookback silently drops late data
when_not: Frequently mutating data without a reliable change marker (use CDC)
resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Quarantine then Publish
resources.description: One bad batch of rows can poison a whole table and every downstream metric.
resources.summary: One bad batch of rows can poison a whole table and every downstream metric.
resources.problem: One bad batch of rows can poison a whole table and every downstream metric.
resources.context: A pipeline where a known fraction of incoming rows may be malformed.
forces: Bad rows must not be silently dropped
Reprocessing bad rows must be possible
resources.solution:
Split every batch into publish and quarantine on a quality contract.
  pass ─▶ published table (SLA-bearing)
  fail ─▶ quarantine table (retained, alertable, reprocessable)
A row never disappears: it is either published or quarantined with a reason.
Alert on quarantine *rate*, not just on a hard failure — a rising rate is the
early signal of an upstream problem.
resources.diagram:
batch ─▶ [contract check] ─┬─ pass ─▶ published ─▶ consumers
                           └─ fail ─▶ quarantine (+reason) ─▶ alert/reprocess
tradeoffs: pro: consumers always read clean data; failures are visible and recoverable
con: extra storage and a reprocessing path to maintain
watch: a quarantine nobody reviews is just a slower data loss

resources.title: Data Vault (hubs, links, satellites)
resources.description: Integrating many changing sources into a warehouse without constant rework.
resources.summary: Integrating many changing sources into a warehouse without constant rework.
resources.problem: Integrating many changing sources into a warehouse without constant rework.
resources.context: Many source systems, frequent schema changes, auditability requirements.
forces: Loads must be parallel and restartable
resources.solution:
Model the raw integration layer as insert-only:
  hubs       — business keys
  links      — relationships between hubs
  satellites — descriptive attributes over time
Loads are insert-only and parallel, so a source change adds a satellite rather
than forcing a rewrite. Build star schemas as a downstream, disposable layer.
resources.diagram:
source ─▶ hub_customer ─┐
         hub_order    ─┼─ link_order_customer ─▶ sat_* ─▶ star marts
source ─▶ hub_product ──┘
tradeoffs: pro: resilient to change, auditable, parallel loads
con: more objects, harder to query directly; needs a downstream marts layer
when_not: A single source feeding a known set of reports

resources.title: Lambda vs Kappa (batch + stream)
resources.description: Streaming is fast but hard; batch is simple but slow; you need both speed and correctness.
resources.summary: Streaming is fast but hard; batch is simple but slow; you need both speed and correctness.
resources.problem: Streaming is fast but hard; batch is simple but slow; you need both speed and correctness.
resources.context: An analytics need with both a latency requirement and a need to reprocess history.
forces: Consistency between batch and stream logic
resources.solution:
Lambda: run a batch layer (authoritative, reprocessable) and a speed layer
(approximate, low-latency), merge at query time. Two code paths, two bugs.
Kappa: one streaming path; reprocessing = replay the log. Simpler, but the log
must retain enough history and the stream must be replay-safe.
Modern default: a single lakehouse path with replayable streams (a pragmatic
kappa), keeping raw immutable so history is always reprocessable.
resources.diagram:
Lambda:  source ─┬─ batch (authoritative) ─┐
                 └─ speed (approx)       ─┴─▶ serve
Kappa:   source ─▶ stream ─▶ table ─▶ serve   (reprocess = replay)
tradeoffs: lambda pro: batch correctness; con: two implementations to keep consistent
kappa pro: one code path; con: requires long log retention + replay safety
when_to_use: Lambda when reprocessing is cheap and latency needs are moderate
Kappa when streams are replayable and ops budget is limited
when_not: Neither, if a nightly batch genuinely meets the SLA — keep it simple

resources.title: Postgres CDC to Lakehouse
resources.description: Batch extraction from an OLTP database loads it and still misses deletes and mid-day changes.
resources.summary: Batch extraction from an OLTP database loads it and still misses deletes and mid-day changes.
resources.problem: Batch extraction from an OLTP database loads it and still misses deletes and mid-day changes.
resources.context: A Postgres/MySQL source whose changes must reach a lakehouse with low latency.
forces: Deletes and updates must be captured
resources.solution:
Read the write-ahead log, not the tables.
  WAL ─▶ Debezium ─▶ Kafka ─▶ [dedupe by LSN] ─▶ MERGE into lakehouse
Rank events by (lsn, ts_ms) so out-of-order delivery resolves deterministically.
Debounce/compact in a streaming job before the merge. Handle tombstones
explicitly (hard or soft delete). Never read the source tables on a schedule.
resources.diagram: Postgres WAL ─▶ Debezium ─▶ Kafka topic ─▶ stream dedupe ─▶ MERGE ─▶ Delta/Iceberg
tradeoffs: pro: low latency, captures updates and deletes, no query load on OLTP
con: operational complexity (slots, connectors, ordering)
watch: a dropped replication slot forces a full re-snapshot
when_not: A nightly batch is sufficient and the source is small

resources.title: Safe Backfill
resources.description: Backfills corrupt production or take down the daily run.
resources.summary: Backfills corrupt production or take down the daily run.
resources.problem: Backfills corrupt production or take down the daily run.
resources.context: A pipeline whose historical output must be recomputed.
resources.solution:
Treat a backfill as a controlled migration.
  1. shadow target (or snapshot)
  2. batched date ranges, smallest first
  3. validate a sample after each batch
  4. swap atomically
  5. keep the old data until validated
Never overlap the production window; never backfill without a rollback path.
resources.diagram: [range] ─▶ shadow ─▶ validate ─▶ swap ─▶ keep old until verified
tradeoffs: pro: reversible, observable, low-blast-radius
con: extra storage and orchestration for the shadow
when_to_use: Any historical recompute of a production table
when_not: A tiny table you can recompute in one safe step

resources.title: Streaming Dedup and Upsert
resources.description: Streaming sinks either duplicate on replay or lose rows on failure.
resources.summary: Streaming sinks either duplicate on replay or lose rows on failure.
resources.problem: Streaming sinks either duplicate on replay or lose rows on failure.
resources.context: A streaming job writing a change/event stream into a mutable table.
resources.solution:
Make the sink idempotent rather than trying to make the source exactly-once.
Deduplicate by a business key + event time within the watermark, then MERGE
(upsert) on the key. A replay recomputes the same rows and merges to the same
state — idempotent by construction. Order by event time, not arrival time.
resources.diagram: stream ─▶ [windowed dedupe by key] ─▶ MERGE (upsert on key) ─▶ table
tradeoffs: pro: correct under replay; no reliance on perfect exactly-once
con: requires a stable business key and event time; state cost
when_not: Pure append-only event log with no dedup need
